content: Rifapentine can reduce the levels or effects of zolpidem by influencing the metabolism of the hepatic and intestinal enzyme CYP3A4. The clinical significance of this interaction is considered minor or unknown. Similarly, rifapentine may decrease the levels or effects of zonisamide through the same enzymatic pathway, with the clinical relevance also being minor or uncertain. However, rifapentine has a serious interaction with zuranolone, reducing its levels or effects via CYP3A4 metabolism. In such cases, alternative medications should be considered. Rifapentine is associated with several adverse effects, including hyperuricemia (likely due to pyrazinamide in combination therapy during the initial phase of tuberculosis treatment), hypertension, headache, dizziness, rash, pruritus, acne, anorexia, nausea, vomiting, dyspepsia, diarrhea, neutropenia, lymphopenia, anemia, leukopenia, thrombocytosis, elevated ALT/AST levels, arthralgia, pain, pyuria, proteinuria, hematuria, urinary casts, and hemoptysis. Hypersensitivity reactions to rifamycins, including severe cutaneous adverse reactions (SCARs) such as Stevens-Johnson syndrome (SJS) and drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS), have been reported. Therapy should be discontinued immediately at the first sign of skin rash, mucosal lesions, or other hypersensitivity symptoms. Rifapentine is not recommended as an initial-phase treatment for HIV-infected individuals with active pulmonary tuberculosis due to a higher relapse rate, particularly in patients with cavitary pulmonary lesions, positive sputum cultures after the initial treatment phase, or bilateral pulmonary disease. The drug may cause a red-orange discoloration of body tissues and fluids, including skin, teeth, tongue, urine, feces, saliva, sputum, tears, sweat, and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF). Contact lenses or dentures may become permanently stained. Cases of porphyria have been reported with rifampin, attributed to the induction of delta-aminolevulinic acid synthetase. Rifapentine may have similar enzyme-inducing properties and should be avoided in patients with a history of porphyria. There are no adequate and well-controlled studies of rifapentine in pregnant women. Limited data from clinical trials involving rifapentine treatment for active or latent tuberculosis suggest no increased risk of spontaneous abortion compared to the general population. However, the quality of adverse event reporting in these trials limits further interpretation. When administered during the last weeks of pregnancy, rifampin (another rifamycin) has been associated with an increased risk of postnatal hemorrhage in both the mother and infant, potentially requiring vitamin K treatment. It is unknown whether rifapentine is excreted in human milk, but similar drugs are known to pass into breast milk. Rifapentine may cause red-orange discoloration of breast milk. A slight increase in rat pup mortality was observed when dams were dosed late in gestation through lactation. A decision should be made to discontinue nursing or the drug, considering the importance of the medication to the mother. Infants exposed to rifapentine through breast milk should be monitored for signs of hepatotoxicity, including irritability, prolonged unexplained crying, yellowing of the eyes, loss of appetite, vomiting, and changes in urine or stool color. Rifapentine inhibits RNA polymerase in Mycobacterium tuberculosis. It has a peak plasma time of 5-6 hours, is 98% protein-bound, and induces enzymes such as CYP3A4 and CYP2C9/10. Its half-life is approximately 13 hours, and it is primarily excreted in feces (70%) and urine. Rifapentine is used in combination with other medications to treat active pulmonary tuberculosis. It may also be used with isoniazid to prevent active tuberculosis in individuals with latent infection (positive TB skin test). It is a rifamycin antibiotic, effective only against bacterial infections and not viral infections like the common cold or flu. This medication should be taken orally with food as directed by a physician, usually once or twice weekly. For optimal efficacy, doses should be evenly spaced. Patients should adhere to the prescribed regimen, even if symptoms improve, to ensure complete eradication of the infection. Common side effects include stomach upset, nausea, vomiting, loss of appetite, and headache. Rifapentine may cause harmless red-orange discoloration of urine, sweat, saliva, or tears, which resolves upon discontinuation. Rarely, it may cause severe intestinal conditions due to Clostridioides difficile infection, which can occur during or after treatment. Severe allergic reactions are rare but possible. Patients should inform their healthcare provider of any allergies, particularly to rifamycins (e.g., rifampin), or other medical conditions. Alcohol consumption may increase the risk of liver disease. Rifapentine may reduce the efficacy of live bacterial vaccines (e.g., typhoid vaccine) and hormonal birth control methods, necessitating alternative contraceptive measures. It may also interfere with certain lab tests, potentially causing false results. In case of overdose, seek emergency medical attention. Routine lab tests (e.g., sputum tests, liver function, bilirubin levels, complete blood count) should be conducted during treatment. Missed doses should be taken as soon as remembered on the same day; otherwise, consult a healthcare provider for guidance. Store rifapentine at room temperature, away from light and moisture. Do not store it in the bathroom. Properly discard expired or unused medication. Always consult a healthcare professional for complete information tailored to individual health needs.
